newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-Slovak GDP growth belie clouds looming.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Slovak GDP growth belie clouds looming.

text.p: The Slovak economy showed strong growth in 1996 despite a turbulent political situation, but analysts warned on Thursday the figures belie a fragile economy that continues to be plagued by structural problems.
On Wednesday, the Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) released detailed figures showing 1996 real GDP growth edged up slightly year-on-year to 6.9 percent from 6.8 percent growth in 1995.
But economists said a lack of deep economic restructuring may come to the forefront over the longer-term, given the growth of imports and sagging exports.

"(The) economic growth is really fragile. The main problem is that it does not create pre-requisites for longer-term, healthier growth," Juraj Rencko, an analyst at the Prognostic Institute of the Academy of Science, told Reuters.
"The imbalanced structure of the economy is the real danger, as it is strongly linked to imports, with the efficiency of the export side lagging far behind," Rencko said.
According to official estimates, GDP growth should slow in the first half of 1997, but is still forecast to show a year-on-year increase of between 5.7 to 6.3 percent.

Analysts said the first half forecast was attainable, but some called for a reduction of growth by a tight fiscal and monetary policies, advising a cautious approach to government investment programmes.
But, said Vladimir Kuklis of bank CSOB, there seems to be too little political will and not enough time until the next elections to achieve such a joint effort.
"Very few people will vote for those who create queues in front of labour officies for unemployment benefits," he said.
The next general elections are scheduled for autumn 1998, and the latest public opinion polls show support for the national-populist ruling coalition of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar to be waning.

"This may be at the heart of the expansive bugdet policy this year because the government will want to employ as many people as possible on projects such as motorway or railway construction," Kuklis said.

The 1997 budget -- forecast to record a 36.9 crown deficit after a 25.5 crown shortfall in 1996 -- has multi-billion crown allocations for infrastructure projects, with only motorway construction expected to cost some 14 billion crowns.
ING analyst Martin Barto said predicted GDP growth for the first half of this year was realistic mainly due to plans for large corporate investments by major companies.

"The good thing about the last year's GDP was the fast increase in investments...and large companies, such as oil refiner Slovnaft, Slovak Telecom or electricty utility Slovenske Elektrarne, have also secured investment funds for this year," Barto told Reuters.
"The real concern, however, is the rapid growth of the state administration consumption," he said adding there were little signs this trend would reverse in 1997.
Meanwhile wage growth, which has so far not seriously threathened the economy, may also become an issue as the elections near.
"Budget expenditure rises with nearing elections in every country, including wage hikes, but this government really cannot afford them," Rencko said.
Wages increased in 1996 grew in nominal terms by 14.6 percent, while industrial output was up a real 2.5 percent, year-on-year. Average inflation in 1996 was 5.8 prercent.

He added the most crucial issue of wage hikes was an eventual increase in export industries, threathening Slovakia's competitiveness on foreign markets and further weakening the trade deficit outlook.
Analysts also said central bank measures at the beginning of the year to reign in credit expansion pushed the cost of money too for companies as well as the government in refinancing its deficit.
